outcome: The general conjecture is unresolved as of 12 October 2026. Since 26 January 2024 two results bear on it: Garonzi and Margolis (arXiv 29 Sep 2025, v2 5 May 2026) prove it for all finite simple groups and all symmetric groups, and a Lean 4 proof of the finite abelian case was posted on 10 Jul 2026 with a commit co-credited to 'Claude Fable 5' (the abelian case was already known, so this is a formalisation). A Steiner-partition paper (Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, June 2025) and a G-harmonic preprint (Aug 2026) address neighbouring questions and do not change the conjecture's status; every later source I found still describes the conjecture as open.
problem_asks: Part (a): G is a group; H_1,...,H_k are subgroups of G of finite index (the statement speaks of 'finite indices'); x_1,...,x_k are elements of G; and the left cosets H_i x_i together partition G (cover G, pairwise disjoint). Part (b), the claim: for every such finite system, the indices [G:H_i] cannot all be pairwise distinct, i.e. there exist i != j with [G:H_i] = [G:H_j]. The claim is universal over all groups G (finite and infinite) and all such finite systems. Two points of wording: the frozen statement does not say k >= 2 or that the H_i are proper, but the literature treats the nontrivial case (k >= 2, proper subgroups), which is what I record; and the literature reduces the general case to finite groups (stated by Garonzi-Margolis and Chouraqui), which I note but do not assume.

events.what_happened: Erdos conjectured in 1950 that an exact covering of the integers by arithmetic progressions must repeat a difference; Mirsky and Newman proved it soon after (Newman and Mirsky never published their proof) and Davenport and Rado independently found the same proof. This is the case G = Z (subgroups nZ of finite index). The original papers were not opened; the attribution comes from the Wikipedia article and the Erdos problems site.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for G = Z only: any exact covering of Z by arithmetic progressions has two progressions with equal difference, i.e. the largest modulus occurs at least twice.
events.remains: Every other group: all other infinite groups and all finite groups.

checked_by.who: Leon Mirsky, Donald J. Newman (proof), Harold Davenport and Richard Rado (independent proof)
checked_by.qualification: The mathematicians credited with the proof
checked_by.what_they_did: Proved the integer case; attribution as given by Wikipedia and the Erdos problems site, not verified against the original papers

events.directly_checkable: The integer case is an elementary covering statement; a finite exact covering of Z can be checked by hand. I did not re-derive the general argument.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to G = Z.

events.what_happened: Znam (1970, Colloquia Mathematica Societatis Janos Bolyai vol. 2, as cited by Wikipedia) proved that in a disjoint covering system of the integers, if the largest modulus n occurs l times then l >= p, where p is the least prime dividing n. Newman (1971, Mathematische Annalen 191, 279-282, 'Roots of unity and covering sets') published a related general result. Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel (Combinatorica 6 (1986) 235-243, DOI 10.1007/BF02579384) gave a non-analytic proof of the Newman-Znam result. Wikipedia's text dates Znam to 1968 and cites the 1970 volume; the sources disagree and I have used 1970. None of the three original papers was opened.
events.delivers: For the integers only (disjoint covering systems of Z): the largest modulus occurs at least p times, p the least prime dividing it. This is a quantitative form of the G = Z case.
events.remains: Every group other than Z; the case of general finite groups.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the 1986 Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the 1986 non-analytic proof of the Newman-Znam result

events.doubts: The year of Znam's paper is inconsistent within the Wikipedia article (1968 in the text, 1970 in the citation).
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to Z; it strengthens the G = Z case.

events.what_happened: Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for finite nilpotent groups', Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 29(3) (1986) 329-333, DOI 10.4153/CMB-1986-050-0. The page states that the note proves the conjecture for finite nilpotent groups. Issue date 1 September 1986; the page shows online publication on 20 November 2018. I read the abstract page only, not the proof.
events.revisions: Online version 20 Nov 2018 (CMB digitisation); the 1986 issue date is taken as the first written argument.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for all finite nilpotent groups (as the paper states its aim; proof not read).
events.remains: Non-nilpotent groups, including non-nilpotent finite solvable and non-solvable groups.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to finite nilpotent groups.

events.what_happened: Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel, 'Remark on the multiplicity of a partition of a group into cosets', Fundamenta Mathematicae 128 (1987) 139-144, DOI 10.4064/fm-128-3-139-144. I read only the journal metadata page, which gives no abstract or theorem. The class of groups is taken from secondary sources: Garonzi-Margolis (cited as 'Berger et al. 1987') and the Erdos problems forum say the conjecture holds for finite groups with a Sylow tower, in particular supersolvable groups.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources only: settles the conjecture for finite groups having a Sylow tower (which includes supersolvable groups). The paper's own statement was not read.
events.remains: Finite groups with no Sylow tower.
events.doubts: The class (Sylow tower) rests on two secondary sources; I did not read the paper's statement.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to groups with a Sylow tower (per secondary sources).

events.what_happened: Zhi-Wei Sun, 'On the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for uniform covers of groups', arXiv math/0306099 (v1 5 Jun 2003; v2 30 Dec 2004), J. Algebra 273(1) (2004) 153-175. For cosets a_i G_i covering G a fixed number of times, with the G_i subnormal and not all equal to G, it shows that the largest number M of indices sharing a common value satisfies M >= the smallest prime divisor of n_1...n_k, and gives min log n_i = O(M log^2 M). Partitions are the multiplicity-one case. Abstract read from the arXiv page.
events.revisions: v1 5 Jun 2003; v2 30 Dec 2004 (17 KB both); journal version J. Algebra 2004.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for partitions in which every subgroup H_i is subnormal in G (the Wikipedia article and the Erdos site both state this case). Because abelian and nilpotent groups have all subgroups subnormal, the abelian case is already covered; the Erdos forum comment of 7 Oct 2025 makes this point.
events.remains: Partitions with at least one non-subnormal subgroup, in any group.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (J. Algebra 273 (2004) 153-175)

events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to subnormal subgroups.

events.what_happened: Yuval Ginosar and Ofir Schnabel, 'Prime factorization conditions providing multiplicities in coset partitions of groups', Moscow Journal of Combinatorics and Number Theory 3(2) (2011) 75-86. The Haifa CRIS record gives the abstract: the conjecture holds for finite groups whose orders admit certain prime factorizations; the main tool is the group-theoretic Chinese remainder theorem. The full text was not available to me.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for finite groups whose order admits certain prime factorisations. The exact conditions are not on the record page; Garonzi-Margolis describe the class as groups whose order is divisible by few primes.
events.remains: Finite groups whose order does not satisfy those factorisation conditions, and infinite groups.

checked_by.who: Moscow Journal of Combinatorics and Number Theory (refereed journal)

events.doubts: The factorisation conditions are unknown to me; the class of groups is described differently by two secondary sources (Garonzi-Margolis; the Erdos forum).
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to finite groups with certain order factorisations.

events.what_happened: Fabienne Chouraqui, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for finitely generated groups', arXiv 1803.08301 (v1 22 Mar 2018; v2 5 Aug 2018, 'Updated version'), Int. J. Algebra and Computation 29(6) (2019) 1083-1112. Works in free groups of finite rank via covering spaces, defines a metric space Y of coset partitions of F_n, gives sufficient conditions for the conjecture, and shows that partitions satisfying them have a neighbourhood in Y where the conjecture also holds. Abstract read from the arXiv page; body not read.
events.delivers: For free groups of finite rank only: the conjecture holds for coset partitions meeting stated sufficient conditions (the conditions were not read). The title says finitely generated groups, but the abstract confines the results to free groups of finite rank.
events.remains: Partitions of F_n not meeting the conditions; all other groups.

checked_by.who: International Journal of Algebra and Computation (refereed journal)

events.direction: Partial, for free groups of finite rank.

events.what_happened: Fabienne Chouraqui, 'The space of coset partitions of F_n and Herzog-Schonheim conjecture', arXiv 1804.11103 (v1 30 Apr 2018, the only version; comment: 'contains the extension of some results in [arXiv:1803.08301]'). No journal reference is listed. The abstract page was read only for its first sentence; the neighbourhood result comes from a search snippet and the body was not read.
events.delivers: For free groups F_n only: per the search snippet, partitions meeting the sufficient conditions of arXiv 1803.08301 have a neighbourhood in the space Y on which the conjecture also holds. Not a proof of any new group class.
events.remains: All partitions outside those neighbourhoods; all other groups.
events.doubts: No journal publication is listed. 'No engagement found' means only that my searches found none; I did not run a citation-index search.
events.direction: Partial and local, for free groups.

events.what_happened: Leo Margolis and Ofir Schnabel, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for small groups and harmonic subgroups', arXiv 1803.03569 (single version, submitted 9 Mar 2018, 16 pages), Contributions to Algebra and Geometry 60(3) (2019) 399-418 (journal reference from a search snippet; not checked on the journal page). Theorem A: every group of order less than 1440 satisfies the conjecture. Theorem B: for n <= 4, every G-harmonic n-tuple of indices is Z-harmonic. The method reduces a counterexample to arithmetic restrictions (Lemmas 2.5-2.6) and Egyptian-fraction-type equations; section 2.3 says that only order 1080 remains after these, and Proposition 4.7 (a 5-tuple) together with Propositions 4.3 and 4.7 closes it. The order-by-order elimination relies on 'elementary computer calculations' that the paper does not display. Read from the ar5iv rendering of the full text; Lemma 4.6 was not verified by me.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for every group of order less than 1440 (finite groups; the paper states the order bound, and the finite reduction covers the general case only as stated in the literature).
events.remains: Finite groups of order 1440 or more; infinite groups, for which the reduction to finite groups is needed.

checked_by.who: Contributions to Algebra and Geometry (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record (publication per search snippet, not checked on the journal page)

checked_by.who: Erdos problems site editors and Alfaiz (forum post 29 Oct 2025)
checked_by.qualification: Site maintainers; not a worked check
checked_by.what_they_did: Cite the result as proved for all groups of order below 1440; the site was updated

events.directly_checkable: Groups of small order can be checked by computer; the paper's own argument uses computer calculations (not displayed), so a reader would need to rerun them.
events.doubts: The order-1080 case rests on a 5-tuple argument (Proposition 4.7) whose long case analysis (Lemma 4.6) I did not verify, and on computer calculations the paper does not show. Two sources (Garonzi-Margolis and the Erdos site) rely on this result as established. A search snippet briefly described order 1080 as still open after the 2018 analysis; the full text, read via ar5iv, closes it.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to groups of order less than 1440.

events.what_happened: Michael C. Burkhart, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for solvable groups', arXiv 1901.10131. v1 (29 Jan 2019, 3 KB) carries the title's claim for solvable groups. v2 (1 Mar 2019, 1 KB) is withdrawn by the author, with the comment: 'The case that a subgroup maps to a full copy of Z_p under the quotient is not trivial and must be considered more carefully.' No reason beyond that comment is given. The abstract as shown on the current abstract page restates the conjecture only; I did not read v1's body.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2019; v2 1 Mar 2019, withdrawn by the author.
events.delivers: Claimed (title only, as far as I read): the conjecture for solvable groups. The claim is withdrawn; I could not confirm what v1 proved.
events.remains: Solvable groups, on this source alone.
events.doubts: The author's own withdrawal comment says a case is 'not trivial and must be considered more carefully'. The solvable-groups claim does not appear in Wikipedia, the Erdos site, or Garonzi-Margolis (as fetched). An earlier search summary said Wikipedia credits Burkhart; the Wikipedia article as fetched does not mention him.

withdrawn.what: v2 withdrawn by the author; the arXiv comment states that one case (a subgroup mapping onto a full copy of Z_p under the quotient) is not trivial and must be considered more carefully. No further reason given.

events.direction: Claimed for solvable groups; withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Fabienne Chouraqui, 'An approach to the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture using automata', arXiv 2001.03882 (v1 12 Jan 2020); Lecture Notes in Computer Science 13257 (DLT 2022) 55-68. Frames the conjecture in terms of Schreier automata of cosets in free groups of rank n >= 2. Theorem 1 gives multiplicity under coprime-period and counting hypotheses; Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5 cover the single-period and two-coprime-period cases; Theorem 2 is conditional on an unproven automata conjecture (Conjecture 1) and passes to all groups by a transfer from an earlier paper of the author. Read from the ar5iv rendering.
events.delivers: Partial: for free groups of rank at least 2 under the stated coprime-period and counting hypotheses, multiplicity holds. The passage to all groups is conditional on an automata conjecture that is not proved.
events.remains: Partitions outside the hypotheses; all other groups; the automata conjecture itself.
events.doubts: The all-groups statement is conditional on an unproven automata conjecture, and the paper says the two conjectures are equivalent only under an extra condition it does not establish.
events.direction: Partial, for free groups; conditional extension to all groups.

events.what_happened: Fabienne Chouraqui, 'Herzog-Schonheim conjecture, vanishing sums of roots of unity and convex polygons', arXiv 2009.04817 (v1 9 Sep 2020, the only version); Communications in Algebra 49(11) (2021) 4600-4615. Recasts coset partitions of free groups as vanishing sums of roots of unity and convex polygons. Theorem 3: multiplicity when the maximal Schreier period h is a prime power p^n or a product p^n q^m. Proposition 4.2(iii): the maximal period repeats at least its smallest prime divisor times; for the integers this recovers the Mirsky-Newman / Davenport-Rado bound, which the paper says it recovers rather than newly proves. Read from the ar5iv rendering and the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Partial, for free groups F_n (n >= 2) whose maximal Schreier period is a prime power or a product of two prime powers. Not a general result; the integer bound is recovered, not new.
events.remains: Periods with three or more prime factors; all other partitions; all other groups.
events.direction: Partial, for free groups with prime-power-type periods.

events.what_happened: Fusun Akman and Papa Sissokho, 'Transversal coset partitions of groups', a preprint hosted by Illinois State University (file name 'Preprint April23', repository upload path dated 2024/05). Per a search snippet of the preprint, the authors prove the Herzog-Schonheim result for 2 <= r <= 7 distinct subgroups, with r = 5 to 7 by computation, and propose a stronger conjecture (for mutually commuting subgroups, at least one subgroup must contribute more than one coset). The PDF could not be read by my fetch tool (returned as binary), so this entry rests on the search snippet. Garonzi-Margolis cite the same title as Beitr. Algebra Geom. 66 (2025).
events.revisions: Preprint dated only by its file name ('April23'), which I have not confirmed on the document itself. Published version reported as Beitr. Algebra Geom. 66 (2025), per Garonzi-Margolis; journal page not opened.
events.delivers: Claimed, per snippet: the conjecture for partitions with 2 to 7 distinct subgroups (cosets). Not a general result.
events.remains: Partitions with 8 or more cosets; all other groups.

checked_by.who: Beitr. Algebra Geom. (journal, per the Garonzi-Margolis reference list)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record, if the reference is correct

events.time_since_posted: about 3 years (if the file-name date is right)
events.doubts: The date and the r range come from a search snippet and a filename; I could not read the PDF.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to 2 to 7 subgroups (per snippet).

events.what_happened: Fusun Akman and Papa Sissokho, 'Steiner coset partitions of groups', Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 68(4) (2025) 1359-1373, DOI 10.4153/S0008439525100787, published online 24 June 2025 (open access). A Steiner coset partition takes exactly one coset from each of several distinct subgroups. The abstract shows no Steiner coset partition exists for four mutually commuting subgroups when G has no C2 x C2 x C2 quotient, and gives explicit Steiner partitions for n-fold direct products of cyclic groups of prime order (n >= 3), lifting to extensions. An erratum (DOI 10.4153/S0008439525101392) corrects the abstract's range for the non-existence statement from any r >= 2 to r in {2, 3}. The abstract says the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture 'remains open'.
events.revisions: Erratum to the abstract (date not established). The first public version of this argument may be the earlier 'Transversal coset partitions' preprint (see akman-sissokho-transversal-preprint); I have used the journal online date and have not resolved which is the first written argument.
events.delivers: Not a result on the conjecture: it concerns Steiner partitions, a structural sub-question with one coset per subgroup of mutually commuting subgroups. It gives non-existence for four such subgroups (corrected erratum range: r in {2, 3}) and explicit constructions; it does not prove any case of the conjecture as stated.
events.remains: The conjecture itself, which the abstract says remains open.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper and an erratum

events.directly_checkable: The explicit Steiner partitions of products of cyclic groups of prime order can be checked by hand for given n.
events.doubts: The abstract's own range was corrected by erratum, which suggests the original claim overreached. The paper's stronger proposed conjecture (at least one subgroup contributes more than one coset) would be contradicted by a Steiner partition; that is a different statement from the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture, but the judging pass should see the distinction.
events.direction: Neighbouring question, discounted: structural non-existence and constructions for Steiner partitions. Neither direction bears on whether indices must repeat, unless the constructions' index pattern is checked.
events.object: Explicit Steiner coset partitions of the n-fold direct product of cyclic groups of prime order, n >= 3, lifting to every extension of that group. The abstract does not say whether the subgroups in these partitions have pairwise distinct indices, which is what would bear on the conjecture; I did not read the body.

events.what_happened: Martino Garonzi and Leo Margolis, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for simple and symmetric groups', arXiv 2509.25118 (math.GR; comment '21p'). Theorem 1.2: the conjecture holds for symmetric groups. Theorem 1.3: it holds for simple groups (finite simple groups via the classification, with infinite simple groups handled as the paper states). Theorem 1.4: for simple S, J(S) = sum over distinct indices m of 1/m tends to 1 as |S| tends to infinity. Method: if J(G) < 2 the conjecture holds, since the reciprocals of the indices of a partition sum to 1; bounds on maximal subgroups; induction for alternating groups; S_n with n <= 6 is taken from Margolis-Schnabel 2018. Computations in GAP and Mathematica, with code in two GitHub repositories (Zenodo DOIs) that I did not open. Presented at seminars in January and February 2026 (search snippets only; not opened). Read from the arXiv abstract page and the HTML of v1 and v2.
events.revisions: v1 29 Sep 2025 17:42 UTC (20 KB); v2 5 May 2026 (26 KB). The paper gives no changelog. The v2 theorem statements (Theorems 1.2-1.4) match v1 as far as I read.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for two classes: all symmetric groups S_n (finite; the paper also covers infinite symmetric groups via the Schreier-Ulam-Baer theorem) and all simple groups (finite simple groups by the classification; infinite simple groups as the paper states). Restricted to these two classes.
events.remains: All other groups: finite non-simple, non-symmetric groups (including solvable and non-solvable groups of order 1440 or more outside those classes), and the general case beyond the finite reduction.
events.directly_checkable: The computations are in two public GitHub repositories (Zenodo-archived), which I did not open; the symmetric and simple-group argument can be checked against the cited maximal-subgroup literature.
events.doubts: No public doubt recorded. Caveats: the S_n result for n <= 6 depends on the 2018 Margolis-Schnabel computations, which the paper does not display; the simple-group result depends on maximal-subgroup bounds from the literature and on GAP calculations, none of which I verified; and no journal version appears (arXiv shows no journal reference as of my fetch). Public uptake so far is the authors' talks and a forum post on the Erdos site (14 Mar 2026) listing the result as proved; neither is a worked check.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to symmetric groups and simple groups.

events.what_happened: Murali Menon, 'Two Questions on G-harmonic Tuples', arXiv 2608.15873 (single version, 16 Aug 2026, 8 pages). Addresses Ginosar's question whether every G-harmonic tuple is Z-harmonic. Reports that Margolis-Schnabel proved this for length at most 4; shows the bound 4 is sharp using the A5-harmonic 5-tuple (6,6,6,10,15), whose associated coset partition of A5 uses only the indices 6, 10 and 15; and shows that no member of a length-5 family analysed by Margolis-Schnabel is G-harmonic for any G. The abstract notes that the repeated indices do not contradict the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture. Read from the abstract page; body and acknowledgements not read.
events.delivers: Answers a neighbouring question (Ginosar's G-harmonic versus Z-harmonic question) negatively at length 5 and shows the length-4 bound is sharp. It does not bear on the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture, whose partitions require pairwise distinct indices and whose examples here repeat indices.
events.remains: The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture in full, untouched by this paper.
events.directly_checkable: The A5 coset partition with indices 6, 10, 15 is explicit and can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Neighbouring question, discounted. Its example is consistent with the conjecture (repeated indices 6, 6, 6).
events.object: An A5-harmonic 5-tuple (6,6,6,10,15) and an associated coset partition of A5 using only the indices 6, 10 and 15; it shows the length-4 bound in Ginosar's question is sharp. Explicit.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository Jostamon/erdos274-hs-abelian (Apache-2.0; 8 commits, all dated 10 Jul 2026). README: 'Lean 4 proof of the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for finite abelian groups (Erdos Problem 274, abelian case)'. Main theorem Erdos274.erdos_274.variants.abelian, matching the formal-conjectures statement. Lean file HerzogSchonheimAbelian.lean has main theorem exists_card_parts_eq_of_commGroup: for a finite commutative group and an exact covering of it by more than one coset (indexed by a finite type with more than one element), there exist distinct i, j with equal cardinality of the parts. Commit 7f3c28f ('Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for finite abelian groups (Erdos 274)') has body: 'A Lean 4 / Mathlib proof of erdos_274.variants.abelian, stated exactly as in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, via a simplified Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel argument. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only. Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>'. The commit's author and committer are shown as 'Jostamon and claude'. Commit 7eaab65 ('Add CI: build and axiom check') carries the same trailer. The README says the proof uses no sorry and no extra axioms, and follows a simplified Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel argument by strong induction on group order; it mentions no AI tool.
events.revisions: 8 commits, all dated 10 Jul 2026; the commit 2ab8a2e is the one the formal-conjectures file pins. The repository creation date is not shown.
events.delivers: A formal proof (Lean 4, Mathlib v4.27.0 per README) of the conjecture for finite abelian groups: for a finite abelian group, any exact covering by more than one coset has two members of equal size, hence equal index. Restricted to finite abelian groups; this is a formalisation of a case already known (Sun 2004 covers it as the subnormal case; Berger et al. 1986 cover nilpotent groups). It adds no new group class.
events.remains: Non-abelian groups, finite and infinite: the conjecture in general, and the non-abelian scope of Erdos problem 274.
events.directly_checkable: The repository builds with elan, lake exe cache get and lake build (per README); it has a CI workflow (commit 7eaab65) for build and axiom check. I did not compile it. The sorry-free status comes from the fetched text of HerzogSchonheimAbelian.lean, which contained no 'sorry' string, and the axiom claim comes from the commit message.
events.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to finite abelian groups.
people: Jostamon (GitHub username; full name not shown)

systems.name: Claude Fable 5
systems.what_it_did: Listed as co-author ('Jostamon and claude') on the commit that adds the Lean proof of the abelian variant (7f3c28f) and on the CI commit (7eaab65). The commit message does not say what the model contributed. The authors' own description of the proof is a Lean/Mathlib formalisation 'via a simplified Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel argument'. Whether the model produced the simplification, the formal proof, or only edits is not stated anywhere I could read; the README says nothing about AI.

events.what_happened: The Erdos problems site's revision log for problem #274 records an edit dated 20 Oct 2025 that appears to narrow the opening question from 'If G is a group' to 'If G is an abelian group'. The log's diff is garbled and I could not reconstruct the full edit. The page remarks that for abelian G the answer to the original question is 'no' and cites Sun [Su04] and Margolis-Schnabel [MaSc19]. Sean Eberhard's forum comment of 7 Oct 2025 says 'This is not open for abelian groups', and suggests dropping 'abelian' and calling the problem the Herzog-Schonheim conjecture. Alfaiz's posts of 29 Oct 2025 and 14 Mar 2026 list the proved cases, including Garonzi-Margolis.
events.revisions: Page last edited 31 Oct 2025 (page footer as fetched).
events.delivers: Not a mathematical result. It changes the problem's stated scope to the abelian case on the site.
events.remains: The non-abelian question as originally posed, under the site's new wording.
events.doubts: The scope of the Erdos problem is itself contested on the site (Eberhard's comment, and the narrowing edit). The edit log is garbled, so the exact wording change is uncertain.
events.direction: Not applicable: site scope change, not a result.

disputes.summary: On the Erdos site the problem #274 wording was narrowed to abelian groups in an edit dated 20 Oct 2025, while Sean Eberhard (7 Oct 2025) argues the question is the general Herzog-Schonheim conjecture and that its abelian case is not open. Whether Erdos #274 is the general conjecture is contested in the record itself, and the Lean abelian result bears on the narrowed wording.

The formal-conjectures entry labels the abelian variant 'solved' while its file contains sorry; the proof lives in the external Jostamon repository at commit 2ab8a2e, which the entry points to. The Erdos site lists 'Formalised statement? Yes' for the same problem, and shows one 'Proof claim' whose content I could not see.

Attribution of the integer case: Wikipedia credits Mirsky and Newman, with Davenport and Rado independently; its Mirsky biography calls the result the Mirsky-Newman theorem, and other sources credit all four. The Wikipedia article gives Znam's year as both 1968 and 1970.

summary: The general Herzog-Schonheim conjecture is open in every source I found, and nothing since 26 January 2024 has settled it. The live development is Garonzi and Margolis (arXiv 2509.25118, posted 29 Sep 2025, v2 5 May 2026): they prove it for all symmetric groups and all simple groups, relying on Margolis-Schnabel 2018 for S_n with n <= 6 and on GAP and Mathematica computations, and no AI system is named in the paper. Their result is not yet in a journal and I found no qualified public check beyond the authors' seminar talks (January and February 2026, from search snippets) and a forum post listing it as proved. The 2018 Margolis-Schnabel result (all groups of order below 1440) is the largest existing case; I checked its order-1080 closure in the full text and it depends on computer calculations the paper does not display. Older partial results are Newman-Znam and Mirsky-Newman (integers), Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel 1986 (nilpotent), Sun 2004 (subnormal), Ginosar-Schnabel 2011 (certain factorisations), and Chouraqui's 2018-2020 free-group results. Burkhart's solvable-groups preprint (2019) was withdrawn by its author with a comment that a case is not trivial, and no later source I read relies on it. The Erdos #274 Lean proof (Jostamon, 10 Jul 2026) formalises the finite abelian case, which is already covered by Sun 2004 as the subnormal case, so it adds a machine-checked proof of a known subcase rather than a new case; the repository's commit trailer credits 'Claude Fable 5' as co-author of that commit, and the README says nothing about AI, so the AI attribution is the authors' trailer alone and does not say what the model contributed. Two close calls: whether Garonzi-Margolis counts as a substantial restricted resolution or as two classes with the general case open (I record it as the latter); and whether the Jostamon AI credit is load-bearing or formalisation of a human argument (I record it in ai.systems and flag the reading). The neighbouring Steiner-partition paper (Akman-Sissokho, CMB June 2025) and the G-harmonic preprint (Menon, Aug 2026) are discounted: neither changes the conjecture's status, and the Menon example repeats indices as the conjecture permits. AI search: no source connects a model to the general conjecture; AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv 2605.22763) solved nine Erdos problems (#12, #26, #125, #138, #152, #741, #846) and #274 is not among them, though I could read only the first half of its text and the attempted list (353 problems) is not in the part I read; Tao's AI-contributions wiki (last updated 30 Jun 2026) has no #274 entry; the Gemini 700-conjecture paper (arXiv 2601.22401) and the FrontierMath Erdos benchmark do not mention #274; the Kourovka paper (arXiv 2607.17477, Aristotle) does not mention Herzog-Schonheim. The Erdos #274 page itself shows no visible status label in the text I fetched, and its 'Proof claim (1)' content is not visible, so I cannot say whether that claim is the Jostamon repository.
competing_reading: For Garonzi-Margolis: a reader could treat it as a large restricted resolution, since all finite simple and symmetric groups are infinitely many groups in which the conjecture now holds, and the authors' method (J(G) < 2) is general; against that, it covers two classes and leaves the general conjecture open. For Jostamon: a reader could treat the abelian Lean proof as a settled variant of Erdos #274 (the formal-conjectures entry says 'solved'), since the abelian case is what the site narrowed the problem to; against that, the case is a formalisation of a 1986/2004 result and the general conjecture is not touched. For the AI credit: a reader could take the 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5' trailer as load-bearing AI involvement in a proof, since the authors credit the model as co-author of the proof commit; against that, the authors' own account says only that the proof is a formalisation of a known argument, and the trailer does not say what the model did, so the contribution may be formalisation work the task says does not count.
what_would_settle_it: For Garonzi-Margolis: a journal version or referee report, any erratum, a citing paper, and an independent rerun of the GAP and Mathematica computations (the two GitHub repositories with Zenodo DOIs, which I did not open). For the Jostamon result: a lake build with an axiom check (CI commit 7eaab65), and a statement from the author of what Claude Fable 5 did in the commits (for example, whether it wrote the Lean proof, the simplification, or only edits). For the AI question on Erdos #274 generally: the full 353-problem attempt list and the Tao wiki entry after 30 Jun 2026. For Burkhart: the v1 body and the reason for withdrawal. For the Akman-Sissokho preprint: the PDF's date and its r-range statement. For Erdos #274 itself: the live status label, the 'Proof claim (1)' content, and the full edit history of 20 Oct 2025.

event.what_happened: Martino Garonzi and Leo Margolis, 'The Herzog-Schonheim conjecture for simple and symmetric groups', arXiv 2509.25118 (math.GR; comment '21p'). Theorem 1.2: the conjecture holds for symmetric groups. Theorem 1.3: it holds for simple groups (finite simple groups via the classification, with infinite simple groups handled as the paper states). Theorem 1.4: for simple S, J(S) = sum over distinct indices m of 1/m tends to 1 as |S| tends to infinity. Method: if J(G) < 2 the conjecture holds, since the reciprocals of the indices of a partition sum to 1; bounds on maximal subgroups; induction for alternating groups; S_n with n <= 6 is taken from Margolis-Schnabel 2018. Computations in GAP and Mathematica, with code in two GitHub repositories (Zenodo DOIs) that I did not open. Presented at seminars in January and February 2026 (search snippets only; not opened). Read from the arXiv abstract page and the HTML of v1 and v2.
event.revisions: v1 29 Sep 2025 17:42 UTC (20 KB); v2 5 May 2026 (26 KB). The paper gives no changelog. The v2 theorem statements (Theorems 1.2-1.4) match v1 as far as I read.
event.delivers: Settles the conjecture for two classes: all symmetric groups S_n (finite; the paper also covers infinite symmetric groups via the Schreier-Ulam-Baer theorem) and all simple groups (finite simple groups by the classification; infinite simple groups as the paper states). Restricted to these two classes.
event.remains: All other groups: finite non-simple, non-symmetric groups (including solvable and non-solvable groups of order 1440 or more outside those classes), and the general case beyond the finite reduction.
event.directly_checkable: The computations are in two public GitHub repositories (Zenodo-archived), which I did not open; the symmetric and simple-group argument can be checked against the cited maximal-subgroup literature.
event.doubts: No public doubt recorded. Caveats: the S_n result for n <= 6 depends on the 2018 Margolis-Schnabel computations, which the paper does not display; the simple-group result depends on maximal-subgroup bounds from the literature and on GAP calculations, none of which I verified; and no journal version appears (arXiv shows no journal reference as of my fetch). Public uptake so far is the authors' talks and a forum post on the Erdos site (14 Mar 2026) listing the result as proved; neither is a worked check.
event.direction: For the conjecture, restricted to symmetric groups and simple groups.

judgement.why: The statement is universal over all groups, so every class-restricted proof is a case. The only post-snapshot event that settles new mathematics is Garonzi-Margolis (simple and symmetric groups): a case, an unreviewed preprint with no specific doubt. The Jostamon Lean repository formalises the finite abelian case, already covered by Berger-Felzenbaum-Fraenkel 1986 and Sun 2004, so its scope is none. Its only AI evidence is a 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5' commit trailer that says nothing about what the model produced, and formalising a known argument is none under Q5 anyway, so ai_role is none. Steiner partitions and G-harmonic tuples are neighbouring questions (variant). Burkhart was withdrawn by its author. Pre-snapshot journal papers are digested cases.
judgement.doubts: The Jostamon AI credit is a bare trailer. If the model devised the 'simplified' argument, that would still be a known case, so it does not change the scope. Akman-Sissokho preprint date (2023) is inferred from a filename.
